🇺🇸 💵 America’s Persian trap: soaring debt, military overreach threaten US’ global supremacy The national debt hit $40.7T, according to new data from the Treasury’s official FiscalData resource. That’s ~$50B more than USDebtClock.org ’s projections, previously disparaged for ‘overestimating’ the amount owed. The debt is projected to hit its $40.1T statutory limit in February or March. Outgoing Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Friday the issue will be left to the new Congress to deal with. If the limit is reached, the Treasury will be barred from issuing new debt , and if the government runs out of cash on hand, spending will be slashed, and benefits, federal and military salaries frozen. Knock-on effects would include credit rating downgrades, spiking interest rates, and if a deadlock is combined with other economic bad news – a steep recession, or worse. The US has been able to amass such a large debt (125% of GDP, ~1/3 of the world’s total government debt) thanks to its “exorbitant privilege” – the dollar’s de facto world reserve currency status, a unique instrument allowing the US to finance deficits and acquire foreign assets using its own currency. But fiscal decline, the rise of alternatives, and the sheer size of the debt have triggered warning signs, such as the 2024 milestone when the US began spending more on debt interest than defense. Economic historian Niall Ferguson postulates that “any great power that spends more on debt service than on defense risks ceasing to be a great power.” That’s doubly true for Washington, whose hard power has traditionally backed its financial and soft power ambitions through its post-Cold War unipolar moment (see Thomas Friedman’s 1999 argument about the “hidden hand of the market” requiring a “hidden fist” of US military power). The Iran war threatens to unravel the US on both fronts, unmasking Washington’s weakened hard power, while triggering an inflationary and spiking interest rate loop that could collapse the housing, stock or bond markets, or inflate the dollar into oblivion. Long term, this would trigger a more a more equitable distribution of global power and resources to the Global South. But short term, it could result in a severe global recession, disrupt trade and trigger massive geopolitical turbulence, from a reordering of global alliances to new regional conflicts for resources and influence. 👍 Substack | Chat | @geopolitics_prime

Last year, Trump tried reaching Kim Jong Un through established phone lines and communications channels. Nobody called back. Trump next wrote a letter. White House officials hatched a plan for a group to wait outside the Manhattan office of North Korea’s permanent mission to the United Nations. When a North Korean diplomat walked past, the group swooped in and thrust the letter into his hands. At a UN meeting, the diplomat later tossed the unopened letter in front of a U.S. representative. Trump also sought a meeting with Kim during his latest Asia trip, but the North Korean leader reportedly set conditions Washington could not accept. Since their last meeting in 2019, North Korea’s nuclear arsenal has grown from an estimated 20–30 warheads to around 60, while Pyongyang has developed intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching the U.S. Kim is now pushing for Washington to recognize North Korea as a nuclear power.
